findings.title: Pin and verify the installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: Every build downloads whatever content the redirected URL serves at build time and executes it as root. A compromised host, redirect, or changed installer can inject arbitrary code into produced images; builds are also non-reproducible.

findings.title: Pin and verify the remote installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: Every image build downloads whatever content is currently served at this mutable URL and pipes it directly into a root shell. A compromised host, DNS path, or changed installer can execute arbitrary code in the build environment and embed it in produced images.

findings.title: Pin and verify the downloaded installer
findings.whyItBreaks: Every build fetches and executes whatever this URL returns, with no version pin or checksum/signature verification. A compromised or changed upstream response becomes arbitrary code execution during image builds and makes builds non-reproducible.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors in LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but this exported API discards it and returns "". Since "" is also a valid stored map value, callers cannot distinguish absence from a present empty value.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failure in the exported wrapper
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but this exported wrapper discards that error and returns "", identical to the valid value for a present key mapped to an empty string. Callers therefore cannot distinguish failed lookup from real data.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key error
findings.whyItBreaks: LoadOrDefault discards ErrMissing and returns "", which is also a legitimate stored map value. As an exported API, every caller is forced to treat a failed lookup as successful retrieval of an empty value.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation could not return until every result was sent. The new goroutines are merely scheduled, so Run can return before any send occurs. A caller that closes results after Run returns will race with these goroutines and can panic with "send on closed channel"; callers also can observe incomplete results after return.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, Run returned only after every result had been delivered. It now launches sends asynchronously and returns immediately. A normal caller that invokes Run and then closes results will close the channel while these goroutines are still sending, causing a "send on closed channel" panic; consumers can also observe incomplete output when Run returns.

findings.title: Keep Run synchronous until all results are sent
findings.whyItBreaks: Run previously completed every send before returning. It now merely launches goroutines, so a caller that closes its result channel immediately after Run returns can cause the goroutines to panic with "send on closed channel". Callers also cannot use return from Run as the completion boundary anymore.

findings.title: Restore admin requirement for record deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: With isAdmin=false and session.tenantId equal to record.tenantId, this returns true, allowing any tenant user to delete any record in that tenant. It also permits an administrator to delete records in a different tenant.

findings.title: Restore admin and tenant checks for record deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing && to || authorizes deletion when either condition alone is true: any non-admin user in the record's tenant can delete it, and an admin from a different tenant can delete it. The prior policy required both authorization and tenant isolation.

findings.title: Require admin status and tenant match for record deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: Using || authorizes any non-admin user to delete every record in their tenant, and authorizes an admin from a different tenant to delete cross-tenant records. The prior check required both authorization conditions.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures instead of overwriting settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Malformed or incomplete stored settings previously threw and prevented save. They now become DEFAULTS; updateFontSize then saves that fallback with the requested size, replacing a user's existing theme/configuration rather than surfacing the invalid input.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures instead of returning defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch conflates malformed JSON and invalid settings fields with legitimate default settings. In updateFontSize, a previously propagated parse/validation error aborted before save; it now saves { theme: "light", fontSize: size }, silently overwriting the user's theme when their stored data is invalid. As parseSettings is exported, external callers also cannot distinguish an invalid input from valid default settings.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures before rewriting settings
findings.whyItBreaks: All JSON and validation failures now become DEFAULTS. updateFontSize then treats that fallback as real settings and saves it. For example, updating font size on {"theme":"dark","fontSize":"14"} now writes {"theme":"light","fontSize":16}, losing the saved dark-theme preference; previously the parse error prevented save from running.

findings.title: Keep report artifacts tied to the requested branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any branch whose ref differs from the "verified" ref, builtFrom reports the branch commit but artifacts are fetched for the verified commit. Consumers can therefore associate artifacts with the wrong build.

findings.title: Use the selected branch commit for artifacts
findings.whyItBreaks: `builtFrom` remains the commit resolved from the caller-selected branch, but `artifacts` are fetched from the unrelated `verified` ref. Reports for a branch can therefore claim artifacts were built from one commit while returning artifacts from another.

findings.title: Fetch artifacts from the reported branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any branch whose ref differs from "verified", builtFrom is the branch commit while artifacts are fetched from the verified commit. The report therefore misattributes artifacts to the requested branch.

findings.title: Restore the requested limit cap
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit smaller than all.length, this returns every reversed entry rather than at most limit. renderFeed passes 20, so inputs with over 20 entries now produce an oversized feed.

findings.title: Restore the positive limit cap
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit smaller than all.length, recentEntries now returns every entry instead of at most limit. renderFeed passes 20 and writes each returned item, so feeds with more than 20 entries now return more than 20 items.

findings.title: Restore slicing to the requested positive limit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit, this returns all reversed entries rather than at most limit. renderFeed calls it with 20 at line 9; when all has more than 20 entries, its loop writes past the preallocated 20-element output and returns an oversized feed.

findings.title: Report the count of rendered entries
findings.whyItBreaks: When any entry is stale, its row is omitted but `# entry-count` remains `entries.length`. Consumers receive a self-contradictory manifest and can reject it or misallocate based on the declared count.

findings.title: Keep header count aligned with emitted rows
findings.whyItBreaks: When any entry is stale, its row is omitted but the unchanged header call still receives entries.length. A manifest with one live and one stale entry therefore declares `# entry-count: 2` while containing one entry row, producing inconsistent output for consumers that use the header count.

findings.title: Count only emitted manifest entries
findings.whyItBreaks: When any entry is stale, its row is removed but `headerLines` still receives `entries.length`, so `# entry-count` claims more records than the manifest contains. Consumers relying on the declared count can reject or misprocess the manifest.

findings.title: Preserve the exported legacy ID formatter
findings.whyItBreaks: Deleting exported Go symbol FormatLegacyID is a source-incompatible API change: any downstream package that still formats persisted or interoperating legacy identifiers will no longer compile on upgrade.

findings.title: Retain FormatLegacyID as a compatibility wrapper
findings.whyItBreaks: FormatLegacyID was an exported package function that produced legacy identifiers. Removing it is a source-incompatible public API change: any downstream module importing example.com/app/ids and calling ids.FormatLegacyID will no longer compile after upgrading.

findings.title: Return the declared string result
findings.whyItBreaks: execute is a public exported function declared to return a string, and previously uppercased its input. It now unconditionally throws, so every consumer receives an exception instead of a result.

findings.title: Restore execute's string-returning behavior
findings.whyItBreaks: execute is exported with a `string` return contract, but every invocation now throws `always fails`; callers can no longer process any input.

findings.title: Restore execute’s declared string-returning behavior
findings.whyItBreaks: execute is publicly exported with the contract `(input: string) => string`, but this implementation unconditionally throws. Every caller is therefore unable to obtain a result for any valid input.

findings.title: Do not reject viewers before read-only handling
findings.whyItBreaks: For an active viewer below the attempt limit, isEligible now returns false, so handle returns "rejected" at line 24. The existing viewer branch at line 25, which returns "read-only", is consequently unreachable.

findings.title: Keep active viewers eligible for read-only handling
findings.whyItBreaks: For an active viewer below the attempt limit, isEligible now returns false, so handle() returns "rejected" at line 24 instead of reaching its existing "read-only" result at line 25. Viewing is a distinct action from processing and is explicitly supported by the handler.

findings.title: Keep viewers eligible for the read-only handler path
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer below the attempt limit now fails isEligible and handle returns "rejected" at line 24. Previously it reached line 25 and returned "read-only", so the new gate blocks an action the handler explicitly supports.

findings.title: Keep saving drafts independent of payment
findings.whyItBreaks: For `{ state: "draft", payment: "missing" }`, the new predicate returns false, so `saveDraft` returns "blocked" at src/actions.ts:9. Saving a draft is the action that should allow an incomplete, unpaid order; payment may legitimately govern submission, but not draft persistence.

findings.title: Allow unpaid drafts to be saved
findings.whyItBreaks: `saveDraft` shares `canProceed`; consequently, `{ state: "draft", payment: "missing" }` now returns `"blocked"`. Saving a draft is the path that must remain available before payment, while the new payment condition only legitimately governs submission.

findings.title: Read files from the requested channel head
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from stable, the returned Snapshot reports commit=repo.headCommit(channel) but files=repo.filesAt(repo.headCommit("stable")). Consumers therefore receive a self-inconsistent snapshot and can publish or inspect stable files while believing they belong to the requested channel.

findings.title: Read snapshot files from the declared commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For a channel whose head differs from stable, the returned Snapshot reports commit=head and channel=<requested channel>, but files are read from stable. Consumers therefore receive content that does not correspond to the snapshot commit.

findings.title: Read snapshot files from the requested channel commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For `publishSnapshot(repo, "feature")`, the returned `commit` is `headCommit("feature")` while `files` are read from `headCommit("stable")`. Whenever those refs differ, the Snapshot describes one commit but contains another commit's files.

findings.title: Honor the new limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: `build(prefix, limit=3)` still returns 10 items because the implementation unconditionally assigns `max_count = 10`. The added public parameter promises caller-controlled result capping but has no effect.

findings.title: Honor the limit argument
findings.whyItBreaks: `limit` promises callers control over result count, but the implementation still iterates over the fixed `max_count = 10`; for example, `build('x', 3)` returns ten entries rather than three. As a public function, this is an unusable contract even without in-repo callers.

findings.title: Honor the new limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: build(prefix, limit=3) still returns ten values because the body iterates the unrelated hard-coded max_count = 10. The added public parameter promises caller-controlled result capping but has no effect.

findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int` now publicly promises a positive result, but `int(value)` accepts `0` and negative inputs. Callers relying on the name to skip their own positivity validation can charge zero or negative amounts; `charge('-1')` returns `-100`.

findings.title: Validate that parsed integers are positive
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int('-2')` returns -2 and `parse_positive_int('0')` returns 0, contradicting its public positive-integer contract. Its caller consequently produces negative or zero charges.

findings.title: Preserve the caller DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation wrote to df.copy() and returned the transformed copy. This change writes directly into df, so callers that retain the input for reuse, comparison, or rollback will observe unexpected in-place value changes.

findings.title: Preserve the input DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation copied df before assigning mapped values. The changed assignment writes directly to df, so callers that retain or reuse their input observe unexpected value changes after calling apply_values.

findings.whyItBreaks: When pinnedTag resolves differently from latest, the changeset advertises fromRevision=from but contains paths computed relative to latest. Consumers replaying those paths on fromRevision can omit required changes or apply an incompatible path set.

findings.whyItBreaks: The Changeset contract states that changedPaths are computed against fromRevision and replayed atop it. This now returns the pinned revision in fromRevision but derives paths using the independently resolved "latest" revision, so a consumer can replay a path set that does not correspond to its declared base revision.

findings.title: Compute changed paths from the advertised revision
findings.whyItBreaks: When pinnedTag resolves to a revision other than latest, changedPaths is computed relative to latest while fromRevision remains the pinned revision. Consumers replaying these paths on top of fromRevision will omit changes between the pinned revision and latest.

findings.title: Restore the missing-settings fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None for a nonexistent path (line 7). The deleted fallback previously supplied workers=1; startup now subscripts None and raises TypeError instead of starting with the established default.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission errors
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit fails, Charge logs the error but returns nil. Its exported API now conflates a failed charge with a successful one, so callers may continue fulfillment or record payment despite no charge completing.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit returns an error, Charge only logs it and returns nil at line 19. Its exported error-returning API therefore makes a failed payment indistinguishable from a successful one; callers can proceed as though the charge completed.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission errors
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit fails, Charge logs the error then returns nil at line 19. Its exported error-returning API therefore makes a failed charge indistinguishable from a successful one, forcing callers to treat rejected or unavailable payments as completed.

findings.title: Include tenantId in the cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: settingsFor still fetches values by tenantId, but all tenants now share one cache entry for a given name. After tenant A reads "theme", tenant B's settingsFor("B", "theme", store) returns A's cached value without calling store.fetch, leaking or misapplying tenant-specific settings.

findings.title: Keep tenant ID in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: settingsFor still fetches values by tenantId, but all tenants now share the cache entry for a given name. After tenant A reads "apiKey", tenant B reading the same name receives tenant A's cached value without calling its store.

findings.title: Retain tenant ID in the cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A caches setting `theme`, a request for tenant B's `theme` reads the same `settings:theme` entry at settingsFor's cache lookup and returns A's value without calling B's store. This breaks tenant isolation and can expose tenant-specific settings.

findings.title: Preserve the exported invalidate parameter contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported API changed from invalidate(tenantId, name) to invalidate(name). Existing TypeScript consumers no longer compile; JavaScript consumers passing the old two arguments silently delete the cache entry for the tenant ID as though it were a setting name, leaving the intended entry cached.

findings.title: Serialize concurrent reservations per SKU
findings.whyItBreaks: Two concurrent calls for the final unit both read remaining=1 before either await completes. Both save 0 and return true, accepting two reservations for one item.

findings.title: Serialize reservations for the same SKU
findings.whyItBreaks: Two concurrent reserve("sku") calls can both read remaining=1 before either await completes, both persist 0, and both return true. The previous synchronous implementation allowed only one successful reservation.

findings.title: Preserve the public Inventory API or version this break
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing consumers using new Inventory() no longer compile because Store is mandatory, and callers expecting reserve() to return boolean now receive a Promise. In JavaScript, a failed reservation Promise is truthy in a synchronous condition, allowing code such as if (inventory.reserve(sku)) to proceed despite no stock.

findings.title: Serialize reservations for the same SKU
findings.whyItBreaks: The await yields before the in-memory count is decremented. Two concurrent reserve("sku") calls after load("sku", 1) both read 1, both save 0, and both return true, reserving two units of one available unit.

findings.title: Preserve the zero-argument Inventory constructor
findings.whyItBreaks: Inventory is exported, and previously supported new Inventory(). Requiring a Store is a source- and runtime-breaking upgrade for every existing consumer, with no compatibility overload or default store.

findings.title: Avoid changing reserve from synchronous to Promise-returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing consumers receive a boolean synchronously. They now receive a Promise, so JavaScript checks such as `if (inventory.reserve(sku))` treat even a failed reservation as truthy; typed consumers also fail assignment/return-type checks.

findings.title: Update retry to consume millisecond backoff values
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff(0) now returns 1,000 milliseconds, but retry still passes backoff(a) * 1000 to its millisecond sleep helper. A first failed attempt therefore waits 1,000,000 ms (about 16m40s) instead of 1 second; capped retries wait 30,000,000 ms (about 8h20m) instead of 30 seconds.

findings.title: Update retry to consume millisecond backoff values
findings.whyItBreaks: `backoff(0)` now returns 1,000 milliseconds, but `retry` still multiplies it by 1,000 before passing it to `setTimeout`. The first retry therefore waits 1,000,000 ms (~16.7 minutes) rather than 1 second; capped retries wait 30,000,000 ms (~8.3 hours).

findings.title: Update retry to consume backoff milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff(0) now returns 1,000 milliseconds, but retry still multiplies it by 1,000 at src/jobs/retry.ts:12. A first failed retry therefore waits 1,000,000 ms (16m40s) instead of the prior and intended 1,000 ms.

findings.title: Propagate the file close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred Close return value is discarded. Previously Save returned f.Close() errors after a successful flush; it now returns nil, so callers cannot detect a failed final file write/close.

findings.title: Propagate the file-close error from Save
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred f.Close() return value is ignored. Previously, after a successful Flush, Save returned f.Close()'s error; it now returns nil when Flush succeeds even if Close reports a delayed write or finalization failure. Callers of this exported API therefore cannot distinguish a completed save from a failed one.

findings.title: Return the file close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred f.Close() return value is ignored. Previously Save returned f.Close()'s error after a successful flush; now callers receive nil when closing the file reports a delayed write or filesystem error, falsely treating the save as successful.

findings.title: Include each page's final row
findings.whyItBreaks: The half-open bounds return end as the first excluded index, but range(start, end - 1) excludes one additional row. Every non-empty page omits its last row; page_size=1 renders every page empty.

findings.title: Include the page end position in the window loop
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns an exclusive end, but range(start, end - 1) excludes both that bound and the final valid row. Every non-empty page loses its last row; a one-row final page becomes empty, so render_page and summarize produce incomplete output.

findings.title: Include the page's final row
findings.whyItBreaks: range's end is exclusive, so subtracting one omits the last row of every non-empty page. A one-row page becomes empty; render_page and summarize consequently produce incomplete output.

findings.title: Restore the cache freshness comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has elapsed time near zero, so it fails `elapsed > ttlMs`, is deleted, and returns null. Conversely, expired entries are returned indefinitely.

findings.title: Do not splice while iterating completed jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an item shifts the next job into its index, but forEach then advances to the following index. Consecutive completed jobs therefore leave every second completed job in the returned queue.

findings.title: Return cache entries before their TTL expires
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has elapsed time near zero, which is not greater than ttlMs. get() now deletes it and returns null immediately; after expiry it instead returns the stale value indefinitely.

findings.title: Do not splice the array while iterating completed jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an element shifts the next job left while forEach advances its index. For [{done:true}, {done:true}, {done:false}], the second completed job is skipped and remains in the result. This also changes the prior non-mutating API behavior by altering the caller's array.

findings.title: Return entries while they are within their TTL
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has elapsed time near zero, so `elapsed > ttlMs` is false; `get` deletes it and returns null. Conversely, expired entries are returned indefinitely.

findings.title: Avoid splicing while iterating completed jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an item shifts the next item into the current index, but `forEach` advances to the next index. For `[done, done, pending]`, the second done job is skipped and remains in the result.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input average result
findings.whyItBreaks: For averageAmount([]), total is 0 and rows.length is 0, so this returns NaN instead of the previous numeric fallback of 0. Callers receiving a number can silently propagate NaN into calculations or output.

findings.title: Do not reorder the caller's rows
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates rows in place. Calling busiest now changes the caller's input order, whereas the previous spread copy preserved it; subsequent display, persistence, or processing using the same array observes reordered data.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input average
findings.whyItBreaks: averageAmount([]) previously returned 0 but now divides 0 by 0 and returns NaN, changing the exported function's behavior for valid empty input.

findings.title: Avoid sorting the caller's array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: busiest now sorts rows in place. A caller that reuses the supplied array observes its order changed after a read-like lookup; previously the function preserved that order.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input average
findings.whyItBreaks: For [], total is 0 and rows.length is 0, so this now returns NaN instead of the previous numeric result 0. The public Row[] signature permits an empty array.

findings.title: Do not reorder the caller's rows
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates rows. Calling busiest now permanently changes the caller's ordering, whereas the prior implementation sorted a copy.

findings.title: Restore numeric ordering when ranking scores
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() without a comparator sorts numeric values lexicographically. For scores [20, 100, 3], reverse produces [3, 20, 100], so topPlayers(..., 1) uses a cutoff of 3 and returns the first input player rather than necessarily the player with score 100.

findings.title: Sort numeric scores with a comparator
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() compares numbers as strings. For players ordered [9, 100, 90] with n=2, rankScores returns [90, 9, 100], yielding cutoff 9; topPlayers then returns [9, 100] and excludes the 90-score player.

findings.title: Sort scores numerically before deriving the cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator sorts numeric values as strings. For players ordered [9, 100, 99] and n=2, rankScores produces [99, 9, 100], yielding a cutoff of 9; topPlayers then returns the first two input players (9 and 100), omitting the 99-score player.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Plain string equality can return after the first differing character, making response time depend on the matching signature prefix. The public handle path exposes a 401-versus-200 signature oracle, so an attacker can use repeated requests to recover a valid HMAC and invoke processor(payload) without knowing the secret.

findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Plain string equality can stop at the first differing character, exposing comparison timing for attacker-controlled signatures. Because a successful verification reaches processor(payload), an attacker can use timing observations to progressively forge the expected HMAC and bypass webhook authentication.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Using == can return after the first differing character, exposing comparison timing to an attacker who can submit repeated webhook requests. The previous hmac.compare_digest implementation was specifically designed to avoid leaking MAC-prefix information; handle() uses this result to authorize processor execution.

findings.title: Keep balance updates in the ledger transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The ledger insert commits when the `with db.transaction()` block exits, but the debit and credit now run afterward. If either balance update fails, the ledger records a completed transfer while balances are unchanged or only the debit is applied. Previously all three writes rolled back together.

findings.title: Keep balance updates in the ledger transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction exits after the ledger insert. If either subsequent balance update fails, the ledger entry is already committed; if the credit update fails after the debit succeeds, funds are removed without being credited.

findings.title: Keep ledger and balance updates in one transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The ledger insert commits when the transaction block exits before `_apply_balances` runs. If either balance update then fails, the transfer returns an error but leaves a committed ledger entry without matching account balances; a failure between the two updates can also leave balances only partially applied.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when deriving billing-day keys
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior implementation derived keys with UTC getters. The new local-time getters produce a different key near midnight for hosts outside UTC; for example, 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z becomes 2025-12-31 in America/Los_Angeles. This changes billing-day classification based on deployment timezone.

findings.title: Keep billing-day keys in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior implementation explicitly derived the key from UTC fields. The new local-time accessors produce a different key for the same instant on hosts in different timezones; for example, 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z becomes 2025-12-31 in America/Los_Angeles. This changes billing-day boundaries and makes results deployment-timezone dependent.

findings.title: Keep billing-day keys in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior implementation explicitly derived the key with UTC getters. The new local-time getters produce a different key depending on the server timezone; for example, under America/Los_Angeles, 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z is now classified as 2025-12-31 rather than 2026-01-01. This can place billing activity in the wrong daily bucket and makes results deployment-timezone dependent.

findings.title: Include tenant in the memoization key
findings.whyItBreaks: After a request for tenant A/account X caches its Profile, a request for tenant B/account X returns tenant A's cached profile without calling fetchProfile. This exposes incorrect cross-tenant data.

findings.title: Keep tenant in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: Two tenants with the same account value share one memo entry. After readProfile("tenant-a", "acct", ...) caches tenant-a’s Profile, readProfile("tenant-b", "acct", ...) returns that cached tenant-a profile without calling fetchProfile.

findings.title: Restore tenant isolation in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: Profiles are fetched by both tenant and account, but the shared memo now uses only account. After reading tenant A's account X, a read for tenant B's account X returns tenant A's cached Profile without calling fetchProfile, exposing incorrect cross-tenant data.

findings.title: Propagate missing-key errors instead of returning an empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: `load` is exported and previously threw for an absent key; it now returns `""`, which is indistinguishable from a legitimately stored empty string. `loadAll` consequently returns partial-looking successful results instead of reporting a missing requested key.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failures
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw `Error("missing: <key>")`; it now returns `""`, which is indistinguishable from an explicitly stored empty string. `loadAll` consequently returns apparently valid values for missing keys instead of reporting the failed lookup.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failures from load
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw `missing: <key>`; it now returns `""`, which is indistinguishable from a legitimately stored empty string. The exported API therefore forces callers to treat failed reads as successful reads, including loadAll.

findings.title: Preserve the existing timeoutMs configuration contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript callers using the exported Config shape `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }` no longer type-check because `timeoutMs` was removed and `retries` is newly required. Existing JavaScript callers still pass `timeoutMs`, leaving `config.timeout` undefined; `Date.now() + undefined` is NaN, so the deadline comparison never stops retries.

findings.title: Surface terminal retry failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When every attempt throws, retryBackground returns `undefined`, exactly as it does after a successful callback. As a new exported API, this forces all callers to conflate exhaustion with success and prevents them from handling the failed background operation.

findings.title: Preserve compatibility for existing retry Config values
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing callers supply the previously required `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }` Config. They now fail TypeScript checking because `retries` and `timeout` are required. JavaScript callers instead produce `deadline = NaN`; the deadline guard is always false, so the configured timeout is silently disabled and all attempts run.

findings.title: Expose exhausted retry failures to callers
findings.whyItBreaks: If every invocation throws, retryBackground catches every exception and returns `undefined`, exactly like a successful call. As a public API, callers cannot distinguish successful completion from all retry attempts failing.

findings.title: Preserve the existing retry Config contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing callers supplying `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }` no longer type-check because `timeout` and `retries` are required. JavaScript callers instead read `undefined` for `timeout`, producing a `NaN` deadline and silently disabling the timeout guard.

findings.title: Make retryBackground execute outside the caller's stack
findings.whyItBreaks: `retryBackground` promises background behavior but invokes `fn()` directly in its synchronous retry loop. A slow or blocking callback therefore blocks the caller for its full execution/retry duration; currently this is just a duplicate synchronous retry implementation.

findings.title: Expose terminal retryBackground failures
findings.whyItBreaks: Every callback exception is discarded and exhaustion/deadline expiry returns `void`, exactly like a successful callback. This exported API forces callers to conflate failure with success.

findings.title: Handle numeric Field values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: `value` is now `string | number`, but `number` has no `length` property. TypeScript rejects this expression, and a JavaScript consumer passing a number would render `len=undefined` rather than its digit count.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported prop contract now permits `value={42}`, but numbers have no `length`; rendering produces `len=undefined` (and TypeScript rejects the property access under normal checking) rather than a valid numeric-field label.

findings.title: Handle numeric Field values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported prop now accepts `number`, but `value.length` is invalid for that union and evaluates to `undefined` at runtime for `value={42}`, rendering `len=undefined` instead of a valid label.

findings.title: Restore the Git output buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: `git diff` at line 140 now inherits Node's 1 MiB `spawnSync` maxBuffer default instead of the previous 64 MiB limit. A PR whose patch exceeds 1 MiB causes the child process to fail, so the review is never produced.

findings.title: Restore the git output buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: The `git` helper now uses `spawnSync`'s default `maxBuffer` (1 MiB), while `runGithub` uses it to collect the complete `git diff` patch. A PR whose patch exceeds that limit causes `spawnSync` to fail before review submission; the previous 64 MiB limit supported such PRs.

findings.title: Restore the git diff buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer restores spawnSync's 1 MiB default. The patch is read through git(["diff", mergeBase, headSha]) at line 140, so a PR diff exceeding 1 MiB now terminates the git child with a buffer error; res.status is then null and this function throws, causing the entire review to fail. The prior 64 MiB limit supported these PRs.

findings.title: Keep the Codex review subprocess read-only
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` lets the invoked Codex configuration/default select a writable sandbox. Since the subprocess runs with `cwd: opts.repoPath`, a review prompt can then cause changes inside the repository being reviewed, violating the caller's read-only review boundary.

findings.title: Keep the Codex invocation read-only
findings.whyItBreaks: Without -s read-only, Codex uses its default workspace-write sandbox. Because this process runs with cwd set to opts.repoPath, an agent run can edit the reviewed checkout or run project commands; those side effects are neither reported through the returned last message nor reverted.

findings.title: Keep Codex execution read-only
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` delegates sandbox selection to the external Codex configuration/default. Since the prompt is passed directly to an agent running with `cwd` set to `opts.repoPath`, a configured writable sandbox can let a review invocation modify the repository, defeating this wrapper's previous non-mutating boundary.

findings.title: Diff from the PR merge base
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA is the current target-branch SHA and that branch advanced after the PR forked, it is not an ancestor of HEAD. `git diff baseSha HEAD` then includes target-only changes as reverse changes, causing the review bundle and changed-path set to include files outside the PR. This can produce incorrect findings and invalid inline review comments.

findings.title: Diff the PR head from its merge base
findings.whyItBreaks: PR_BASE_SHA can be a newer base-branch commit that is not an ancestor of the PR head. `git diff baseSha HEAD` then compares both trees and includes base-branch-only changes, while ignoring the already-computed `PR_HEAD_SHA`. In a checkout of a merge ref or another revision, the bundle is also analyzed from `HEAD` but posted against `headSha`, so findings can describe a different commit than the reviewed PR.

findings.title: Restore the PR merge-base and configured head SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: A PR branch may fork before its base branch advances. Diffing the current base tip directly against HEAD includes those unrelated base-branch changes as reverse changes, so the review bundle and inline-comment path set no longer describe only the PR. This also ignores PR_HEAD_SHA: when Actions checks out a merge ref or another commit, the review is generated from HEAD but posted against headSha, so findings can target a different revision.

findings.title: Preserve literal prompt payloads during replacement
findings.whyItBreaks: `String.prototype.replace` interprets `$&`, `$`` , `$'`, and `$$` in a string replacement. A reviewed patch containing a literal `$&` (common in regex-related source) is injected as `{{PATCH}}` rather than `$&`; other tokens splice prompt-template text into the patch. The critic therefore receives a corrupted diff and can produce an incorrect review.

findings.title: Preserve literal prompt payloads during replacement
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace treats `$&`, `$'`, `$`` and `$$` in a string replacement as substitution tokens. A bundle field, candidate finding, or patch containing such text is therefore altered before it reaches the review/critic prompt; for example `$&` becomes `{{BUNDLE}}` or `{{PATCH}}`, and `$'` injects the remaining template suffix. The previous callback replacements preserved these payloads literally.

findings.title: Preserve literal prompt content during replacement
findings.whyItBreaks: String.replace interprets `$&`, `$`` , `$'`, and `$$` in a string replacement. Bundle JSON includes the raw patch, so a reviewed patch containing (for example) `$&` is transformed into the placeholder text instead of being sent literally. The same corruption can affect critic findings and patch content, producing reviews of altered input.

findings.title: Keep the fallback review pinned to the reviewed SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: When the initial review POST fails, this fallback omits commit_id. GitHub then defaults the review to the PR's most recent commit, while this run generated its result from the previously captured headSha. If a commit is pushed between analysis and the fallback request, a pass or changes-requested review is recorded against code that was never reviewed.

findings.title: Keep the reviewed SHA in the fallback request
findings.whyItBreaks: When the JSON review request fails and the PR receives another commit before the fallback runs, omitting commit_id makes GitHub attach the fallback review to the PR's then-current head. Its REQUEST_CHANGES verdict was computed from headSha captured at src/adapters/github.ts:141, so it can block the newer commit for findings that no longer apply. Previously the fallback remained attached to the reviewed SHA.

findings.title: Keep the fallback review pinned to the reviewed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When the first POST fails and the PR receives a new commit before the fallback runs, omitting commit_id makes GitHub attach the fallback review to the PR's most recent commit. The review body was computed from headSha and its corresponding diff, so it can approve or request changes on code that was never reviewed. Previously the fallback was pinned to headSha.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of defaulting them
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid or incomplete producer output now becomes a returned Finding: for example, an unknown severity becomes P1, and a missing file/line/reason/fix becomes empty strings and line 0. Previously these inputs threw validation errors. Callers of this exported parser can no longer distinguish malformed review data from a real finding, and may display or act on an unlocatable fabricated P1 finding.

findings.title: Preserve the exported strict-mode normalization option
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the exported strict parameter is a source-compatible API break for existing TypeScript consumers calling normalizeReview(raw, false). In JavaScript, the extra argument is ignored and the previous best-effort behavior of dropping invalid findings is replaced by manufacturing defaulted findings.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: A review containing `findings: [{}]` used to fail validation (invalid severity, then required-field checks). It now succeeds with a synthetic P1/bug finding whose file and explanation fields are empty and whose line is 0. Callers cannot distinguish malformed model output from a real review result and can display or act on invalid review locations.

findings.title: Restore the strict parameter's filtering behavior
findings.whyItBreaks: This removes the public `strict` parameter. Existing TypeScript callers of `normalizeReview(raw, false)` no longer compile; JavaScript callers silently get different results because invalid findings were previously omitted in non-strict mode but are now retained as fabricated defaults.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of defaulting them
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid severities/categories and missing required location/explanation fields previously caused normalizeReview to fail. They now become seemingly valid P1/bug findings at an empty file and line 0, so consumers cannot distinguish malformed review output from an actual finding.

findings.title: Keep the repository explicit when resolving manual PR refs
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow_dispatch path reaches these commands before the Checkout PR head step. Without -R (or GH_REPO), gh pr view must infer a repository from the current directory, but no checkout has established a repository there. It therefore cannot resolve the supplied PR number; the command substitutions yield no SHA output, so the subsequent checkout/review receives empty refs instead of the requested PR.

findings.title: Keep an explicit repository for manual PR ref lookup
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so this branch runs before actions/checkout. gh pr view without --repo (or GH_REPO) resolves its repository from a local Git repository; no checkout has occurred and this workflow no longer supplies REPO. The commands therefore cannot reliably resolve the PR and write empty head/base outputs, preventing the advertised manual review path from checking out the requested PR.

findings.title: Restore explicit repository selection
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so this pre-checkout branch runs. Removing -R leaves gh pr view without a repository context or GH_REPO; no checkout occurs until line 42. gh therefore cannot resolve the requested PR on a clean runner, producing empty refs or failing the run. [GH_REPO documentation](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_help_environment)

findings.title: Restore malformed review failures
findings.whyItBreaks: This exported normalizer previously rejected missing or wrongly typed top-level fields. It now maps malformed input such as null or {} to a valid RawReview with an empty summary and arrays, which is indistinguishable from a legitimate empty review. Callers can therefore report or persist a failed/malformed model response as a successful no-findings review.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-review failures
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid or incomplete review payloads previously threw a malformed-output error. They now return an indistinguishable empty review (empty summary/findings/checked/residual risks), so callers cannot distinguish a failed parser/model response from a legitimate no-findings review and may treat it as a successful pass.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-output errors
findings.whyItBreaks: Missing or invalid required fields now become empty values instead of rejecting the response. For example, a model response lacking findings, checked, or residual_risks is indistinguishable from a legitimate review with no findings or risks, allowing malformed output to be treated as a clean review.

findings.title: Restore PR-ref resolution for manual dispatches
findings.whyItBreaks: `workflow_dispatch` events have no `pull_request` payload. Consequently both SHA variables are empty, while checkout falls back to the workflow’s selected `github.ref` and the base fetch falls back to `main`, neither of which is derived from the supplied `pr_number`. A manually dispatched review can therefore run the wrong tool revision/base and passes empty PR SHAs instead of the requested PR’s refs.

findings.title: Resolve requested PR refs for workflow dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is absent. The checkout therefore falls back to github.ref rather than the supplied pr_number's head; lines 45-46 likewise pass empty base/head SHAs, and line 35 fetches main rather than the selected PR's base branch. A manual review can consequently run against the wrong revision instead of the requested PR.

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for manual dispatches
findings.whyItBreaks: `workflow_dispatch` events have no `pull_request` payload. These expressions therefore provide empty base/head SHAs, checkout falls back to the workflow's `github.ref` rather than the requested `pr_number` head, and the base fetch defaults to `main` even for PRs targeting another branch. Manual reviews consequently run against incorrect or missing PR refs.

findings.title: Preserve capacity for large git diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: runLocal reads the complete `git diff` output through this helper (line 100). Without the former 64 MiB `maxBuffer`, spawnSync uses Node's 1 MiB default; a larger patch fails with a max-buffer error, `res.status !== 0`, and the local review aborts instead of producing a review.

findings.title: Preserve the git diff output buffer
findings.whyItBreaks: `runLocal` reads the complete `git diff` into `patch` at line 100. Without `maxBuffer`, `spawnSync` uses Node's 1 MiB default; a larger diff terminates with a max-buffer error, `res.status` is nonzero/null, and `git()` throws instead of producing a review. The previous 64 MiB limit supported these inputs.

findings.title: Restore the buffer limit for git diff output
findings.whyItBreaks: `runLocal` obtains the complete review patch through `git(["diff", ...])` at line 100. Without `maxBuffer`, Node's `spawnSync` default is 1 MiB; a larger diff terminates with a buffer error, so no bundle or review result is produced. The previous 64 MiB limit supported these inputs.

findings.title: Keep review execution failures as failed checks
findings.whyItBreaks: A thrown review error now creates a completed check with conclusion "neutral" instead of "failure". Neutral is accepted as a non-failing required-check conclusion, so a PR can satisfy the Needlefish check requirement even though no review completed; the human-readable summary cannot be used by branch protection to distinguish this failure.

findings.title: Scope the PR diff command to the target repository
findings.whyItBreaks: `gh pr diff` infers its repository from the process working directory, but this adapter identifies the target via `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` and uses its `cwd` argument for local repository data. When those directories differ, the bundle can contain the diff for the same-numbered PR in another repository (or fail), while its metadata and review posts target `GITHUB_REPOSITORY`.

findings.title: Keep review failures as failing checks
findings.whyItBreaks: When review() or review publication throws, the adapter still exits nonzero but creates the named Needlefish check with conclusion "neutral". GitHub treats this as a non-failing outcome, so a required Needlefish check can cease blocking a PR precisely when no review result was produced.

findings.title: Restore a checkout containing the review tool
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR-head checkout is the workspace, but this repository tree contains only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json; it has no package.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, node_modules, or src/cli.ts. Consequently pnpm install fails before review, and the CLI path would also be absent.

findings.title: Do not execute the PR checkout as the reviewer
findings.whyItBreaks: For any same-repository PR, these changes install dependencies and execute src/cli.ts from the attacker-controlled head commit on a self-hosted runner while GH_TOKEN has pull-requests: write and checks: write permissions. A PR author can alter package lifecycle metadata or src/cli.ts to run arbitrary commands, compromise runner state, and use the token to modify PR/check data.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Keep the reviewer checkout trusted
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR head is checked out into the workspace, then its package manifest/lockfile is installed and its src/cli.ts is executed. An internal PR can add a lifecycle script or alter the CLI to execute arbitrary commands on the self-hosted runner and use GH_TOKEN, which has pull-request and checks write permissions. It can also forge or suppress its own review result.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Restore a runnable reviewer checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The repository tree contains only this workflow and .needlefish/answers.json; it has no package.json, lockfile, node_modules, or src/cli.ts. The workflow therefore cannot execute the specified reviewer command, so every review job fails instead of producing a PR review.

findings.title: Keep the reviewer code outside the PR checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: After checking out the PR head, this command executes src/cli.ts and dependencies supplied by that PR. A same-repository PR can replace the reviewer with code that always reports PASS or uses the injected GH_TOKEN to write forged checks/reviews, defeating the review gate. The removed trusted checkout previously prevented this.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Preserve canonicalization of incoming severity values
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped external input and routes every finding through normalizeFinding. A prior-compatible value such as " p1 " or "p2" now fails the exact enum check and is emitted as P3, silently downgrading a real finding's severity instead of preserving its canonical P1/P2 value.

findings.title: Preserve case-insensitive severity normalization
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped raw review JSON and passes each finding through this function. A severity previously accepted as equivalent to a valid value, such as "p0" or " P1 ", now fails the exact-membership check and is emitted as P3. This silently downgrades real high-severity findings instead of preserving their stated severity.

findings.title: Keep GitHub tokens out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the explicit environment scrub makes spawnSync inherit process.env, including GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN. The invoked `codex exec` process can read those credentials despite its read-only filesystem sandbox; prompts commonly include untrusted repository content, so prompt-injected commands can disclose or use the repository's GitHub token.

findings.title: Keep GitHub tokens out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the sanitized env makes `spawnSync` inherit `GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and `GITHUB_API_TOKEN`. The prompt-driven Codex subprocess can now read credentials that the previous implementation explicitly withheld, including when CODEX_BIN is configured to another executable.

findings.title: Keep GitHub tokens out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the explicit env scrub makes spawnSync inherit GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN. runCodex passes its prompt directly to a tool that can execute commands in the reviewed repository; a malicious prompt or repository instruction can read and exfiltrate those credentials. The read-only sandbox does not prevent environment-variable disclosure.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository guard for the self-hosted job
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork PRs can now run this job on the self-hosted runner. The workflow checks out the fork-controlled head SHA (line 23), runs its dependency installation (line 28), and executes its checked-out TypeScript (line 34). A fork author can therefore execute arbitrary code in the runner environment and potentially access runner-resident credentials or tamper with subsequent jobs.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository guard before running PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork PRs now pass through a checkout of github.event.pull_request.head.sha and execute attacker-controlled dependency installation and src/cli.ts on a self-hosted runner. A fork author can alter package lifecycle metadata or the CLI source, gaining code execution in the runner environment.

findings.title: Restore the fork guard before running PR-controlled code
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork pull requests now enter this self-hosted job, which checks out the fork-controlled head SHA and executes both `pnpm install` and `tsx src/cli.ts`. A contributor can modify the checked-out package metadata, lockfile, or source to execute arbitrary commands on the runner.

findings.title: Preserve explicit zero-duration configuration
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, an explicit value of "0" was accepted and passed to the two runner shutdown timers. It now falls back to 5000 ms for NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS and 2000 ms for NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS, so existing deployments configured for immediate escalation or immediate give-up will unexpectedly wait seconds longer.

findings.title: Preserve zero-valued runner duration settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing deployments that set NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 or NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 now receive the 5000 ms or 2000 ms fallback instead. Those values directly control the delay before SIGKILL and before resolving a timed-out runner, so an explicit immediate action is silently changed into a multi-second delay.

findings.title: Preserve zero-valued runner durations
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously valid values of `0` for `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS` and `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS` scheduled their respective follow-up actions immediately. This change rejects `0` and silently substitutes 5000 ms or 2000 ms, changing behavior for existing deployments configured to skip either delay.

findings.title: Deep-review every changed file
findings.whyItBreaks: Only the six highest-risk mapped hotspots are reviewed. A large PR can contain more than six distinct mapped surfaces; all files belonging solely to later hotspots are omitted from deep review. The removed tail-coverage hotspot previously added every uncovered changed file.

findings.title: Preserve deep-review residual risks
findings.whyItBreaks: Blocking residual risks returned by deep reviewers are replaced with an empty array before the critic runs. The critic and final deriveVerdict call therefore cannot distinguish an incomplete/unverifiable deep review from a fully reviewed PR, allowing a PASS despite a deep reviewer reporting blocks=true.

findings.title: Preserve partial results when a deep review fails
findings.whyItBreaks: A rejected or malformed deep-review call now rejects reviewLarge outright. Previously, the failure was caught and returned as a blocking residual risk while other hotspots continued, so one transient model failure no longer prevents a large PR from receiving a review result.

findings.title: Forward deep-review residual risks to the critic
findings.whyItBreaks: Residual risks returned by successful deep passes are discarded and replaced with []. The critic therefore cannot distinguish a review with unresolved blocking evidence from one with no risks, and deriveVerdict receives only any newly invented critic residuals. This can turn an intentionally blocked large review into a PASS.

findings.title: Deep-review every changed file outside selected hotspots
findings.whyItBreaks: Only the first six mapped hotspots are reviewed. Removing the uncovered-file tail means a large bundle whose mapper returns more than six disjoint hotspots, or omits a changed file, silently skips those files entirely and can report a clean review without inspecting their diffs.

findings.title: Preserve blocking residual risks from deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: Each successful deep review can report a blocking residual risk, but this replacement always gives the critic an empty residual_risks array. The critic can therefore return no residual risk, and deriveVerdict will emit a pass despite a deep reviewer having explicitly reported incomplete, blocking evidence.

findings.title: Deep-review every changed file omitted by selected hotspots
findings.whyItBreaks: Large reviews retain only six mapped hotspots and no longer add a coverage hotspot for changed files absent from those selections. Such files never reach a deep-review prompt; the critic receives only patchStat and no base/head revision identifiers, so it cannot inspect their diff to recover the missed review.

score.error: malformed critic output: finding was not in the candidate review

findings.title: Preserve focus when constructing large-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: Unlike reviewSmall, reviewLarge no longer forwards bundle.focus to either the map bundle or each deep-review prompt. A caller requesting review of a specific concern receives an unscoped large-PR review instead; the removed deep-prompt replacement also leaves any {{FOCUS}} placeholder in the loaded prompt unresolved.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For durations from 119500ms through 119999ms, minutes is floored to 1 while the remainder rounds to 60 seconds, so rendered output is `1m 60s` rather than `2m 0s`. The same invalid representation occurs at every minute boundary.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For a duration such as 119999 ms, minutes is floored to 1 while the remainder rounds to 60 seconds, so rendered review statistics say "1m 60s" rather than "2m 0s". This affects both per-call and total-duration output.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For 119500ms, minutes is floored to 1 while the remainder rounds to 60 seconds, producing `1m 60s`; the prior logic correctly rounded the total to 120 seconds and displayed `2m 0s`. This affects rendered per-call and total timing output.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: `parsePositiveInteger("0", label)` now returns `0`, contradicting both its exported name and its error contract that promise a positive integer. Public callers can rely on this validator before passing the value to an operation that requires a strictly positive count or limit.

findings.title: Reject zero in the positive-integer parser
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed guard accepts "0" and returns 0, although the exported function name and its error contract promise a positive integer. Public callers may safely rely on a result being greater than zero; this change makes that invariant false.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: parsePositiveInteger's exported name and error message promise a positive integer, but this condition returns 0 successfully. Public callers can therefore receive an unvalidated zero where the API promises a value greater than zero.
